prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a party waives the right to compel arbitration by substantially utilizing the litigation machinery to the prejudice of the other party.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The District Court Correctly Held That [Movant] Waived Any Right to Compel Arbitration by Substantially Using the Litigation Machinery.

#### A. Waiver turns on the movant's litigation conduct, not on a showing of prejudice.

The right to arbitrate, like any contractual right, can be waived. This Court has long held that a party waives it by "so substantially utiliz[ing] the litigation machinery that to subsequently permit arbitration would prejudice the party opposing the stay." *Maxum Founds., Inc. v. Salus Corp.*, 779 F.2d 974, 981 (4th Cir. 1985); *see also* *Am. Recovery Corp. v. Computerized Thermal Imaging, Inc.*, 96 F.3d 88, 95 (4th Cir. 1996); *MicroStrategy, Inc. v. Lauricia*, 268 F.3d 244, 251 (4th Cir. 2001); *Forrester v. Penn Lyon Homes, Inc.*, 553 F.3d 340, 342–43 (4th Cir. 2009); *Rota-McLarty v. Santander Consumer USA, Inc.*, 700 F.3d 690, 704 (4th Cir. 2012). The inquiry is fact-specific. It considers the length of the delay, the extent of the movant's litigation activity, and the effect on the opposing party. *See* *Patten Grading & Paving, Inc. v. Skanska USA Bldg., Inc.*, 380 F.3d 200, 204–05 (4th Cir. 2004); *Chorley Enters., Inc. v. Dickey's Barbecue Rests., Inc.*, 807 F.3d 553, 563–64 (4th Cir. 2015).

The Supreme Court has since confirmed that waiver of the right to arbitrate is governed by ordinary waiver principles and does not require a showing of prejudice. *Morgan v. Sundance, Inc.*, 596 U.S. 411, 417–19 (2022). The question is whether the movant knowingly relinquished the right by acting inconsistently with it. *Id.* at 419. To the extent this Court's earlier decisions treated prejudice as a separate requirement, *Morgan* displaced that portion of them. Waiver is established here under either formulation.

#### B. [Movant] acted inconsistently with the right to arbitrate.

[Movant] filed [its complaint / answer and counterclaims] in federal court without invoking the arbitration clause. It then spent [__] months litigating on the merits. During that time it [moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) and obtained a ruling; served [__] interrogatories and [__] document requests; took [__] depositions; and negotiated and submitted a joint Rule 26(f) report and scheduling order]. [Movant] first mentioned arbitration only after [an adverse ruling / the close of discovery / the filing of Defendant's dispositive motion]. JA__.

This is the conduct *Maxum* and its progeny describe. A party that seeks the court's judgment on the merits, and tests the strength of its case with discovery and motion practice, cannot later move the dispute to a different forum if the result disappoints. *See* *Am. Recovery*, 96 F.3d at 95–96; *Patten Grading*, 380 F.3d at 204–05. [Movant] knew of the arbitration clause from the outset because it drafted it. A movant's full awareness of its contractual right makes inconsistent conduct more probative of intentional relinquishment. *See* *Morgan*, 596 U.S. at 419.

#### C. Compelling arbitration now would also prejudice Defendant.

Even if prejudice were still required, the record establishes it. Prejudice may arise from delay, from duplicative expense, or from the use of litigation devices that give the movant advantages unavailable in arbitration. *See* *Forrester*, 553 F.3d at 343; *Rota-McLarty*, 700 F.3d at 704. Defendant has incurred approximately $[__] in fees responding to [Movant]'s motion and discovery. Defendant has also disclosed its [witnesses, damages theory, and trial strategy] in discovery. [Movant] used the [Rule 12 ruling / discovery] to refine its own position. Compelling arbitration now would require Defendant to repeat much of this work, and it would reward [Movant] for using the court as a testing ground. This Court has recognized that late invocation of arbitration, after a party has sought and used the benefits of litigation, is the kind of prejudice that supports a finding of waiver. *See* *Maxum*, 779 F.2d at 981; *MicroStrategy*, 268 F.3d at 251.

#### D. The cases finding no waiver are distinguishable.

Decisions rejecting waiver involved movants who invoked arbitration promptly or whose litigation activity was minimal, defensive, or required by the court. *See, e.g.*, *MicroStrategy*, 268 F.3d at 251; *Patten Grading*, 380 F.3d at 205–06. [Movant] did not act promptly, and its activity was neither minimal nor defensive. [Movant] initiated the merits litigation and pursued it for [__] months.

The Court should affirm the district court's finding of waiver.
